title: Inside the PS2 Slimline redesign: less volume, fewer chips, new trade-offs
summary: Sony's 2004 redesign integrated networking and progressively combined core silicon, but its dramatic size reduction removed the original expansion bay and changed serviceability.

sourceLabels.sony-slim-announcement: PlayStation 2 gets a slimmer, lighter and network-ready redesign
sourceLabels.sony-ee-gs-chip: Emotion Engine and Graphics Synthesizer become one chip

blocks.text: A console reduced to a fraction

The SCPH-70000 family replaced the original PS2's tall expansion-bay chassis with a body dramatically smaller and lighter. This was not empty plastic removed around identical boards. Years of semiconductor and board revisions had reduced chip count and power, allowing Sony to shorten traces, simplify cooling and reorganize the optical mechanism.

Sony had already announced a process for combining Emotion Engine and Graphics Synthesizer functions into one package. Later revisions continued consolidating support logic. Each integration step removed packages, pins and board area while reducing manufacturing cost. The Slimline was the consumer-visible result of a long cost-engineering program, not a single miniaturization trick.

Ethernet became standard on the Slim, eliminating the separate rear adapter for broadband play. That made online setup simpler and ensured new buyers had the physical port. The network controller still appeared through the PS2's DEV9 environment to software, preserving the programming boundary even though the hardware arrangement changed.

The thin chassis had no space for the original 3.5-inch hard drive and Network Adapter assembly. That mattered for the official HDD and Final Fantasy XI in regions where the game required it. A redesign that improved the typical owner's experience therefore removed a capability important to a smaller, committed audience—one reason model numbers matter in PS2 history.
Thermals and power changed by revision

Early Slim systems used an external power brick, moving heat and bulk outside the case; the later SCPH-90000 family returned the supply inside. Cooling paths, laser assemblies and lid sensors also evolved. Repair advice cannot safely treat every ‘Slim’ as identical because a fix, replacement part or thermal assumption may apply only to one board family.

Sony aimed to preserve the enormous software library, but integration can expose titles that relied on accidental timing or undocumented behaviour. Later boards also removed the i.LINK port found on early fat models. Most owners saw a smaller PS2; developers and preservationists saw a set of subtly different targets under one retail name.
A redesign that prolonged the platform

Lower material and shipping costs helped Sony sell PS2 alongside its successor for years. The Slimline made the established library easier to place in new households, while the missing bay marked the end of the original machine's expansion vision. Its success shows how late-generation engineering can reshape a platform without changing the discs on store shelves.
